title: API gateway
short: One front door that checks every request, then routes it.
what: Big apps are split into many services, but the phone app shouldn't need to know them all. An API gateway is the one address every request goes to. It checks who you are, applies limits, and forwards the request to the right service.
analogy: The front desk of an office building. Visitors sign in once at the desk and get sent to the right floor. Each office doesn't run its own security.

frames.say: Three services sit behind one gateway. The phone app only knows one address, api.shop.com. Each path prefix maps to a service.
GET /orders/42 arrives with a login token. The gateway checks the token first, so no service has to repeat that work.
Next, the rate limit. User 7 has made 38 of the 100 calls allowed per minute, so the request may go on.
The path starts with /orders, so the gateway forwards it to the Orders service. The app never learns where Orders really lives.
GET /search/shoe goes to Search. If Search is later split in two, only the gateway's route table changes, not the app.
A request with no valid token stops here with 401. A user over 100 calls a minute gets 429. The services never see either one.

when: Many services behind one public address
Every request needs the same login and rate limit checks
Phone and web clients call the same backend
You want to move or split services without changing the app
output:
/orders/42    orders-svc
/search/shoe  search-svc
/orders/42    401 no token
/users/7      users-svc
/orders/43    429 too many calls
/cart         404 no such route
cost: Find the route for a path
watch: The gateway is one door for everything: run several copies behind a load balancer.
Keep business logic out of it. It routes and checks; the services decide.
Every request pays one extra hop, so keep its work small and fast.
interview: Design an online store backend with many services
Design the backend for a ride-sharing app
